svg.title: Why pushing harder stops helping: pressure along a narrowed airway, with no applied PEEP
svg.desc: Simplified teaching model with illustrative numbers, not patient data; pressures in cm H2O relative to atmospheric pressure at the airway opening, where the mouth is 0 because no PEEP is applied in any panel. Three stacked panels each show an airway running from an alveolus on the left, past a thick line marking the chest wall, to the mouth on the right, with an arrow for expiratory flow toward the mouth and a pressure scale beneath. Panel A, quiet passive expiration: pleural pressure −6, lung recoil 7, alveolar pressure +1; airway pressure falls from +1 at the alveolus to 0 at the mouth and stays above the dashed pleural line, and a label gives transmural pressure of +7 at the alveolus to +6 at the large airways, held open. Panel B, forced expiration through a narrowed airway: pleural pressure +20 inside the chest and 0 beyond the chest wall, recoil 10, alveolar pressure +30. Airway pressure falls along the direction of flow through +30, +26, +20, +12 and +4 to 0 at the mouth, with transmural pressures of +10, +6, 0, −8 and −16. A red dashed line marks the equal pressure point, where inside equals pleural pressure at +20; upstream of it arrows on the wall point outward, and downstream the wall is drawn narrowed with arrows pointing inward. A dotted line shows a normal airway under the same effort, +30, +29, +27, +25 and +20, reaching +20 only in a stiff central airway. Panel C, harder effort through the same narrowed airway: pleural pressure +40, recoil still 10, alveolar pressure +50; airway pressure falls through +50, +46, +40 at the equal pressure point, +24 and +8 to 0, with transmural pressures of +10, +6, 0, −16 and −32. Brackets show that the drop from the alveolus to the equal pressure point is still 10, equal to recoil, with every upstream pressure 20 higher, while the drop from the equal pressure point to the mouth rises from 20 to 40, the extra 20 spent across the compressed segment; the flow arrow is labeled flow unchanged, flow-limited. An inset plots expiratory flow in L/s against expiratory effort as pleural pressure, without effort values: three curves rise and then level off, a normal airway at 5 L/s, a narrowed airway at 1 L/s and, dotted, the narrowed airway at higher lung volume, with more recoil and wider airways, at 2 L/s, with a note that the plateau is about recoil divided by upstream resistance: 10/2, 10/10 and 15/7.5.
